note: Wren Phonics — SEND small-step framework (generic, applies to any GPC) plus 4 fully worked examples spanning Phase 2 (m), Phase 3 (sh), Phase 4 (CCVC words — a word structure, no new sound) and Phase 5 (a-e, a split digraph). Every worked example's model word is re-checked decodable at the exact day that grapheme is first taught. provenance: Wren original, b410, 2026-10-08.

framework.name: Say it
framework.detail: Adult models the pure sound alone, 3 times. Child echoes each time before anything else happens — no letter, no picture yet, just the sound.

framework.name: See it
framework.detail: Show the grapheme together with its picture-cue mnemonic. Point to the grapheme while saying the sound again, so eye and ear connect to the same sound at the same moment.

framework.name: Feel it
framework.detail: Feel the sound being made (a hand on the throat for a voiced sound, a puff of air on the palm for p or t), then air-write the letter large and write it once with a pencil on paper, saying the sound each time — more repetitions than a mainstream lesson would use. Not sand, foam or dough: they pull attention away from the letter (DfE validation Note 8; Reading Framework p.55).

framework.name: Do it
framework.detail: Repeat the grapheme's own physical action several times, slowly at first, building speed only once the action itself is secure.

framework.name: Blend it
framework.detail: Blend the sound into exactly ONE already-known word, very slowly, sound-button by sound-button, before trying anything harder — do not introduce a second word until the first is secure.

framework.name: Check it
framework.detail: Child says the sound back correctly, unprompted, on request, at least 3 times across the session (not 3 times in a row at the end) before the session is counted as a pass.

entry.pronunciation_note: A closed-lip hum held for a moment — 'mmm', not 'muh'.
entry.mnemonic: Milo the mushroom hums happily under the shady tree all day long — 'mmm, mmm'.

character.name: Milo
character.blurb: Milo is a round, spotty mushroom who loves cool, shady corners of the garden and hums to himself all day.

entry.formation_cue: Start at the top of the small letters. Pull straight down, go back up, over in a hump and down, back up and over in a second hump and down. Finish on the line.
entry.action: Press your lips together and hum a long 'mmm' while patting both cheeks gently, like Milo humming to himself.

entry.pronunciation_note: A soft, quiet sound you can hold, 'shhh' — like asking for quiet, no vowel added on the end.
entry.mnemonic: Shelly the snail slides into her shell and whispers shhh when the garden gets too noisy.

character.name: Shelly
character.blurb: Shelly is a shy snail who tucks into her shell and hushes everyone with a soft shhh.

entry.formation_cue: Write 's', then 'h', close together — two letters, one sound.
entry.action: Hold one finger up to your lips and whisper shhh.

entry.label: CCVC words
entry.title: Two consonant sounds together at the start
entry.explanation: Words that start with two consonant sounds, like stop and frog. Say every sound, then blend: s-t-o-p, stop. For a sound you can hold (s, f, l), hold it and slide into the next one.

entry.pronunciation_note: This is another way to write the same sound children already know as 'ai' in rain and 'ay' in day — here the letters split apart around a consonant, so it's called a split digraph.
entry.mnemonic: Echo Star sits at the far end of the word and can't shout her own name — instead she beams her light back over the consonant in between to wake up the 'a' and make it say its own name, 'ay'.

character.name: Echo Star
character.blurb: Echo Star sits quietly at the end of the word, and instead of making her own sound, she beams her light backwards to wake the letter across the gap.

entry.formation_cue: This sound splits in two: write 'a', then a consonant in the middle, then 'e' right at the end — like cake, where 'a' and 'e' are two ends of a bridge with 'k' standing on it.
entry.action: Children point to an imaginary letter far ahead, then mime a beam travelling backward from their fingertip to their other hand, saying 'ay' as it arrives.
